claims.text: The high corrosion resistance of dual-phase stainless steels is primarily caused by rapid formation and maintenance of a chromium-rich passive oxide film.
High grain-boundary and phase-interface densities accelerate chromium diffusion to the steel surface.
Selective dissolution of iron contributes to chromium enrichment and oxidation in the passive film.
Severe plastic deformation can produce an ultrafine-grained stainless-steel microstructure.
The proposed grain-refining treatment increases grain-boundary density without changing the overall alloy chemistry.
Aqueous 0.6 M NaCl and high-temperature NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 molten salts are representative environments for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, respectively.
Enhanced grain-boundary and phase-interface density produces a self-healing, continuous, chromium-enriched passive oxide film.
Preferential dissolution establishes a local chemical-potential gradient that drives chromium from the bulk to the surface.
Surface chromium oxidizes to form a protective film that slows subsequent corrosion.
Ultrafine-grained samples will form a thicker chromium-rich oxide film than coarse-grained samples.
Ultrafine-grained samples will form a more uniform and stable chromium-rich oxide film than coarse-grained samples.
Ultrafine-grained stainless steels will have significantly lower corrosion rates than coarse-grained controls under identical conditions.
A minimum chromium concentration is necessary for passivation by the proposed mechanism.
The proposed passive-film mechanism remains governing across typical chemical-processing and nuclear-power temperatures, salt compositions, and stress states.
Extreme environmental variations or radical alloy-composition changes may alter the corrosion mechanism.
Chromium can undergo substantial depletion from DS2205 during high-temperature molten-salt exposure.
Failure of the ultrafine-grained samples to improve both chromium-rich film formation and corrosion rate relative to coarse-grained controls would falsify the hypothesis.
